Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(A_j)_{j\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint. For each $j$, let $I_j:=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\in A_j\}$. The sets $I_j$ are pairwise disjoint, and at most $n$ of them are nonempty, because each index $i$ belongs to at most one $I_j$. Their union is $\{i:x_i\in\bigcup_jA_j\}$. Hence the number of sample indices in $\bigcup_jA_j$ is $\sum_j\#I_j$, and dividing by $n$ gives $P_n(\bigcup_jA_j)=\sum_jP_n(A_j)$.
Steps 1.1–1.2 show that $P_n$ is a nonnegative countably additive set function with total mass one; by [F2] it is a probability measure.

Let $n\ge1$, let $T_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a total statistic, and fix a sample $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. For $0\le m\le n$, define its maximum replacement displacement by

$$B_m(T_n,x):=\sup\bigl\{|T_n(y)-T_n(x)|:y\in\mathbb R^n,\ \#\{i:y_i\ne x_i\}\le m\bigr\}\in[0,+\infty].$$

When the set is nonempty, the finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is

$$\epsilon_n^*(T_n,x):=\frac1n\min\{m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:B_m(T_n,x)=+\infty\}.$$

Only coordinate replacements are counted, and the replacement values range over all of $\mathbb R$. This is a property of the statistic at the fixed sample; it is not a probability or contamination-neighborhood statement.

derivations.claim: With no replacements the mean displacement is zero. Replacing coordinate $i$ by $M$ changes the sample mean to $\bar x+(M-x_i)/n$, whose displacement is unbounded as $M\to+\infty$. Thus the smallest breaking count for the mean is one, and [F1] gives $1/n$.

Let $n=2r+1$. If at most $r$ coordinates are replaced, at least $r+1$ original observations remain. Writing $x_{\min}=\min_i x_i$ and $x_{\max}=\max_i x_i$, at least $r+1$ resulting observations are at most $x_{\max}$ and at least $r+1$ are at least $x_{\min}$. Therefore the $(r+1)$-st order statistic lies in $[x_{\min},x_{\max}]$, so its displacement from the original median is bounded uniformly over all such replacements.

Replace $r+1$ coordinates by the same value $M>x_{\max}$. The $r$ unchanged observations are the first $r$ order statistics and the $r+1$ copies of $M$ occupy positions $r+1$ through $2r+1$. The median is therefore $M$, which is unbounded as $M\to+\infty$.
Steps 1.2–1.3 show that the smallest breaking count for the odd-sample median is $r+1$. By [F1] its breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/(2r+1)=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\mathcal P$ be a collection of probability measures on it, and let $T:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a single-valued map with finite $k\ge1$. Such a map is a **statistical functional**. For $F\in\mathcal P$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, suppose the point-contamination path $F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x$ belongs to $\mathcal P$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$ ([[def-gross-error-path]]). The **gross-error influence function** at $(x;T,F)$ is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F):=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{T(F_{\epsilon,x})-T(F)}{\epsilon}\in\mathbb R^k,$$

when this finite right limit exists. Its domain may be a proper subset of $\mathcal X$.

derivations.claim: For $t\in I$, the mean value theorem [F3] gives $|\psi(y-t)-\psi(y-\theta)|\le |t-\theta|g(y)$ for $F$-almost every $y$, so $J(t)$ is finite. For any $t\in I$ and nonzero $h$ with $t+h\in I$, the difference quotient of $\psi(y-t)$ in $t$ converges pointwise to $-\psi'(y-t)$ and is bounded in absolute value by $g(y)$, again by [F3]. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $J'(t)=-\int\psi'(y-t)\,dF(y)$. If $t_j\to t$ in $I$, continuity of $\psi'$ gives pointwise convergence of $\psi'(y-t_j)$ to $\psi'(y-t)$, and the same majorant with [F2] shows $J'(t_j)\to J'(t)$. Thus $J$ is $C^1$ on $I$.

Define $H_x(e,t):=(1-e)J(t)+e\psi(x-t)$ for real $e$ near $0$ and $t\in I$. By step 1.1 and $\psi\in C^1$, $H_x$ is $C^1$; also $H_x(0,\theta)=0$ and $\partial_tH_x(0,\theta)=J'(\theta)=-A\ne0$. Applying [F4] gives a unique local $C^1$ root $t=\theta_x(e)$ through $(0,\theta)$. For $e\ge0$ small, [F1] identifies its equation with the stated M-location equation under $F_{e,x}$.

At $(0,\theta)$, $\partial_eH_x=\psi(x-\theta)-J(\theta)=\psi(x-\theta)$ and $\partial_tH_x=-A$. The derivative formula in [F4] therefore yields $\theta_x'(0)=\psi(x-\theta)/A$. Since a two-sided derivative implies the same right derivative, [F5] identifies this value with $\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)$.
If $\psi(u)=u$, then $J(t)=\int y\,dF(y)-t=\mu-t$, so its unique root is $\theta=\mu$ and $A=\int1\,dF=1$. Substitution in step 3.1 gives $\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=x-\mu$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\mathcal P$ be a collection of probability measures on it, and let $T:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a single-valued map with finite $k\ge1$. Such a map is a **statistical functional**. For $F\in\mathcal P$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, suppose the point-contamination path $F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x$ belongs to $\mathcal P$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$ ([[def-gross-error-path]]). For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

derivations.claim: Since $I$ is open, $f$ is continuous at $m$, and $f(m)>0$, choose $\delta>0$ and $c>0$ so that $[m-\delta,m+\delta]\subset I$ and $f(u)\ge c$ throughout this closed interval. For $s<t$ in it, the density identity gives $F(t)-F(s)=\int_s^t f(u)\,du\ge c(t-s)>0$. Thus $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing there, with $F(m)=1/2$.

Suppose first that $x<m$, and shrink $\delta$ so that $m-\delta>x$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, the number $r_\epsilon=(1/2-\epsilon)/(1-\epsilon)$ lies strictly between $F(m-\delta)$ and $1/2$. Continuity and strict increase give a unique $q_\epsilon\in(m-\delta,m)$ with $F(q_\epsilon)=r_\epsilon$. Since $r_\epsilon\uparrow1/2$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, for every $0<\eta<\delta$ eventually $r_\epsilon>F(m-\eta)$, so $m-\eta<q_\epsilon<m$ and $q_\epsilon\to m$. Since $q_\epsilon>x$, the mixture cdf at $q_\epsilon$ is $(1-\epsilon)F(q_\epsilon)+\epsilon=1/2$. For $t<x$, the contamination term is zero and, by monotonicity and $F(m)=1/2$, the mixture cdf is $(1-\epsilon)F(t)\le(1-\epsilon)/2<1/2$. At $t=x$, monotonicity gives $F(x)\le F(m-\delta)<r_\epsilon$, so $(1-\epsilon)F(x)+\epsilon<(1-\epsilon)r_\epsilon+\epsilon=1/2$. For $x<t<q_\epsilon$, the contamination term is $\epsilon$ and $F(t)<F(q_\epsilon)=r_\epsilon$: below the local interval this follows from monotonicity and $F(t)\le F(m-\delta)<F(q_\epsilon)$, and inside it from strict increase. Therefore the mixture cdf at such $t$ is $(1-\epsilon)F(t)+\epsilon<(1-\epsilon)r_\epsilon+\epsilon=1/2$. Together with the cases $t<x$ and $t=x$, this puts the mixture cdf below $1/2$ for every $t<q_\epsilon$, while it equals $1/2$ at $q_\epsilon$, so [F2] gives $m(F_{\epsilon,x})=q_\epsilon$.

If $x>m$, shrink $\delta$ so that $m+\delta<x$. For small $\epsilon>0$, $s_\epsilon=1/(2(1-\epsilon))$ lies strictly between $1/2$ and $F(m+\delta)$. There is a unique $q_\epsilon\in(m,m+\delta)$ with $F(q_\epsilon)=s_\epsilon$. Since $s_\epsilon\downarrow1/2$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, for every $0<\eta<\delta$ eventually $s_\epsilon<F(m+\eta)$, so $m<q_\epsilon<m+\eta$ and $q_\epsilon\to m$. Now $q_\epsilon<x$, so the mixture cdf at $q_\epsilon$ is $(1-\epsilon)F(q_\epsilon)=1/2$. For every $t<q_\epsilon$, the contamination term is zero; if $m\le t<q_\epsilon$, strict increase on the local interval gives $F(t)<F(q_\epsilon)$, and if $t<m$ then monotonicity gives $F(t)\le F(m)<F(q_\epsilon)$. Thus the mixture cdf is below $1/2$ for every $t<q_\epsilon$, while it equals $1/2$ at $q_\epsilon$, so [F2] gives $m(F_{\epsilon,x})=q_\epsilon$.

In the case $x<m$, step 2.1 gives $F(q_\epsilon)-F(m)=-\epsilon/[2(1-\epsilon)]$ and $q_\epsilon\to m$. The density identity and continuity of $f$ imply $[F(q_\epsilon)-F(m)]/(q_\epsilon-m)\to f(m)$. Dividing these two relations yields $(q_\epsilon-m)/\epsilon\to-1/(2f(m))$.
In the case $x>m$, step 2.2 gives $F(q_\epsilon)-F(m)=\epsilon/[2(1-\epsilon)]$ and $q_\epsilon\to m$. The same density quotient tends to $f(m)$, hence $(q_\epsilon-m)/\epsilon\to+1/(2f(m))$.

If $x=m$, continuity of $F$ at $m$ gives $F_{\epsilon,m}(m-)=(1-\epsilon)/2<1/2$ and $F_{\epsilon,m}(m)=(1+\epsilon)/2>1/2$. Monotonicity then puts every $t<m$ below the median threshold, while $m$ itself is above it, so the lower median remains exactly $m$ and its right derivative is $0$. By [F3] and steps 3.1–3.2, these three cases give the displayed pointwise influence function.

The absolute influence value is $1/(2f(m))$ for every $x\ne m$ and zero at $m$. Both sides of $m$ are nonempty in $\mathbb R$, so the supremum over all directions is $1/(2f(m))$ by [F4]. Since $F$ has a density near $m$, $F\{m\}=0$; therefore the conventional expression $(1/2-\mathbf1\{x\le m\})/f(m)$ agrees with this pointwise derivative $F$-almost everywhere, though its value at $x=m$ is not the literal right derivative.

Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\theta\in\mathbb R$ satisfy

$$J(\theta):=\int\psi(y-\theta)\,dF(y)=0.$$

Assume $\int|\psi(y-\theta)|\,dF(y)<\infty$ and that there is an open interval $I$ containing $\theta$ and a nonnegative $g\in L^1(F)$ such that $|\psi'(y-t)|\le g(y)$ for $F$-almost every $y$ and every $t\in I$. Put $A:=\int\psi'(y-\theta)\,dF(y)$ and assume $A\ne0$. For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, let $\theta_x(\epsilon)$ be the locally unique root near $\theta$ of

$$\int\psi(y-t)\,dF_{\epsilon,x}(y)=0,\qquad F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x.$$

Then, for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$, this local root exists and

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{\theta_x(\epsilon)-\theta}{\epsilon}=\frac{\psi(x-\theta)}{A}.$$

Here $T(F_{\epsilon,x})$ denotes this local root. In the special case $\psi(u)=u$ and $F$ has a finite first absolute moment, $\theta=\mu:=\int y\,dF(y)$ and $\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=x-\mu$.

For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

For any fixed sample $x\in\mathbb R^n$, the sample mean $\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$. If $n=2r+1$ is odd and the conventional sample median is the $(r+1)$-st order statistic, its finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/n=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the mean influence function exists for every $x\in\mathbb R$ and equals $x-\mu$.
The sample-mean replacement breakdown fraction is $1/n$ by [F3], independently of the distribution $F$.
The values $|x-\mu|$ are unbounded as $x$ ranges over $\mathbb R$; hence [F2] gives $\gamma^*(T,F)=+\infty$.
Thus in this example the population gross-error sensitivity is infinite, while one arbitrary coordinate replacement already makes the finite-sample mean unbounded.

Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $m=m(F)$ be its lower median, and assume $F(m)=1/2$. Suppose that on an open interval $I$ containing $m$ there is a continuous density version $f$ satisfying

$$F((s,t])=\int_s^t f(u)\,du\quad(s<t,\ s,t\in I),\qquad f(m)>0.$$

For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the right point-contamination influence function of the lower-median functional is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;m,F)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x<m,\\[4pt]0,&x=m,\\[4pt]+\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x>m.\end{cases}$$

Consequently, its gross-error sensitivity is $\gamma^*(m,F)=1/(2f(m))$.

For any fixed sample $x\in\mathbb R^n$, the sample mean $\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$. If $n=2r+1$ is odd and the conventional sample median is the $(r+1)$-st order statistic, its finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/n=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the influence values have absolute value at most $1/(2f(m))$, and their supremum is exactly that value, which is finite because $f(m)>0$.
By [F2], the finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/(2r+1)=1/2+1/[2(2r+1)]$.
Since $1/[2(2r+1)]\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, the odd-sample median breakdown fractions tend to $1/2$.
The bounded pointwise sensitivity and the separate replacement count follow from different definitions and theorems; here the median has both properties under the stated density hypothesis.

A degenerate law cannot satisfy the positive continuous density premise.

Statement: The proof uses the supplied F,m,f,n and selects no family.

Example: a breaking fraction approaching one half does not imply the clean law has a positive median density; the population sensitivity hypotheses and sample breakdown calculation are separately stated.

If f(m)=c>0, every median IF value has magnitude at most 1/(2c).

The sample statistic is the middle order statistic for odd n=2r+1; its first breaking count r+1 gives 1/2+1/[2(2r+1)]. This includes n=1, ties and fixed arbitrary samples; limit is through odd n, independent of the population law. No iid or uniform contamination result is inferred. Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $G$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$, and put $F_G(t):=G(( -\infty,t])$. For any $G$ such that $S_G:=\{t\in\mathbb R:F_G(t)\ge1/2\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, define its **lower median** by

$$m(G):=\inf S_G.$$

The stated condition makes $m(G)$ a finite real number. This convention chooses the left endpoint when the set of medians is an interval; it assumes neither a density nor uniqueness.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\mathcal P$ be a collection of probability measures on it, and let $T:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a single-valued map with finite $k\ge1$. Such a map is a **statistical functional**. For $F\in\mathcal P$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, suppose the point-contamination path $F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x$ belongs to $\mathcal P$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$ ([[def-gross-error-path]]). The **gross-error influence function** at $(x;T,F)$ is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F):=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{T(F_{\epsilon,x})-T(F)}{\epsilon}\in\mathbb R^k,$$

when this finite right limit exists. Its domain may be a proper subset of $\mathcal X$.

For probability measures $F,H$ on a common measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and $0\le\epsilon\le1$, the gross-error path is $F_{\epsilon,H}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon H$, a probability measure by [[lem-convex-mixture-of-probability-laws]]. For any $x\in X$, its point-contamination direction at $x$ is the specialization $H=\delta_x$ ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]). The path is used for a derivative at $\epsilon=0$; the definition alone gives no uniform-in-$H$ remainder.

For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

Let $n\ge1$, let $T_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a total statistic, and fix a sample $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. For $0\le m\le n$, define its maximum replacement displacement by

$$B_m(T_n,x):=\sup\bigl\{|T_n(y)-T_n(x)|:y\in\mathbb R^n,\ \#\{i:y_i\ne x_i\}\le m\bigr\}\in[0,+\infty].$$

When the set is nonempty, the finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is

$$\epsilon_n^*(T_n,x):=\frac1n\min\{m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:B_m(T_n,x)=+\infty\}.$$

Only coordinate replacements are counted, and the replacement values range over all of $\mathbb R$. This is a property of the statistic at the fixed sample; it is not a probability or contamination-neighborhood statement.

Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $m=m(F)$ be its lower median, and assume $F(m)=1/2$. Suppose that on an open interval $I$ containing $m$ there is a continuous density version $f$ satisfying

$$F((s,t])=\int_s^t f(u)\,du\quad(s<t,\ s,t\in I),\qquad f(m)>0.$$

For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the right point-contamination influence function of the lower-median functional is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;m,F)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x<m,\\[4pt]0,&x=m,\\[4pt]+\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x>m.\end{cases}$$

Consequently, its gross-error sensitivity is $\gamma^*(m,F)=1/(2f(m))$.

Let $n=2r+1\ge1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$. Let $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical probability law and write $x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(n)}$ for the sorted sample. Then the lower median $m(P_n)$ is $x_{(r+1)}$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

derivations.claim: By [F14], every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable; since [F5] makes $[-1,1]$ Borel and Lebesgue measurable with measure $2$, each $A\cap[-1,1]$ is measurable for Borel $A$. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $A_j$, these intersections are disjoint, so countable additivity of $\lambda$ gives countable additivity of $P(A)=\lambda(A\cap[-1,1])/2$. Also $P(\varnothing)=0$ because $\lambda(\varnothing)=0$, and $P(\mathbb R)=1$ by [F5]. Thus [F1] and [F2] make $P$ a Borel probability law. For $-1\le t\le1$, [F5] gives $F_P(t)=P((-\infty,t])=(t+1)/2$; for $t<-1$ the intersection $(-\infty,t]\cap[-1,1]$ is empty. It follows that $m(P)=0$, the density near zero is $f=1/2$, and $P$ has no atoms, the latter by the degenerate-interval case of [F5].

Fix any point $z\in\mathbb R$. By [F9], $P_{\epsilon,z}$ is carried by a bounded interval containing $[-1,1]$ and $z$, and its only possible atom location is $z$, because [F5] gives $P(\{z\})=0$. The trigger in $T$ requires two distinct atom locations, so it is false and $T(P_{\epsilon,z})=m(P_{\epsilon,z})$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$. Therefore [F8] and [F12] give $\operatorname{IF}(z;T,P)=\operatorname{IF}(z;m,P)$, equal to $-1$ for $z<0$, $+1$ for $z>0$, and $0$ for $z=0$.

Fix odd $n=2r+1\ge5$ and a clean sample $x\in[-1,1]^n$. Its empirical median is the middle order statistic by [F13] and lies in $[-1,1]$, so every atom location of $P_n$ is within distance $2$ of that median. The trigger is false and $T_n(x)$ is the sample median.

After at most one replacement, at least $n-1=2r$ observations remain in $[-1,1]$. At least $r+1$ resulting observations are at most $1$ and at least $r+1$ are at least $-1$, so the middle order statistic, hence the lower empirical median by [F13], remains in $[-1,1]$. All unchanged atom locations are within distance $2$ of it, and only the single replacement can add a distinct outlying atom. Thus the trigger is still false and $T_n$ remains the sample median in $[-1,1]$ for every one-coordinate replacement; its maximum displacement is bounded.
The absolute values in step 1.2 have supremum $1$ over $z\in\mathbb R$, so [F10] gives $\gamma^*(T,P)=1<\infty$.

Replace two coordinates by distinct values $M$ and $2M$ with $M>3$. The remaining $2r-1$ observations lie in $[-1,1]$, so the middle order statistic (position $r+1$) is still one of them and lies in $[-1,1]$; by [F13] this is the lower empirical median. Both new atom locations are more than $2$ above that median, so the trigger is true and $T_n=2M$. Letting $M\to+\infty$ makes the maximum displacement unbounded. Since step 1.4 ruled out one replacement and [F11] defines the first unbounded count, the breakdown fraction is exactly $2/n$.

Along odd $n\to\infty$, $2/n\to0$, while step 2.1 gives finite gross-error sensitivity at the fixed law $P$. Hence this functional has bounded influence and an empirical plug-in statistic whose replacement breakdown is not bounded away from zero, refuting the Statement.
